newsitem.title: USA: Dollar edges higher as FOMC meets.
newsitem.headline: Dollar edges higher as FOMC meets.

text.p: NEW YORK, Feb 4 - The dollar edged higher Tuesday, but gains were limited as traders awaited the end of a meeting of Federal Reserve policy-makers, the release of key U.S. employment data and a weekend gathering of world financial leaders.
Supportive comments by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and a German newspaper article reporting the United States was considering a missile strike against Iraq helped boost the dollar, traders said.
The Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's policy arm, began a two-day meeting Tuesday, with any announcement on monetary policy not expected until Wednesday afternoon.

While most economists predicted the central bank will leave short-term interest rates unchanged, investors were cautious about pushing the dollar sharply higher before the results of the meeting are known.
"People want to be careful," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Bank Julius Baer and Co.

Investors also adopted a guarded posture ahead of the release Friday morning of potentially market-moving U.S. employment figures for January and before a meeting Saturday in Berlin of finance ministers and central bank heads of the Group of Seven leading industrial powers.

The world financial leaders from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Japan, Italy and the United States are expected to discuss the currency market, including the dollar's impressive gains against the yen and mark.
In late New York trading Tuesday, the dollar fetched 1.6457 German marks, up from 1.6400 marks Monday. The dollar rose to 122.40 Japanese yen, up from 121.70 yen.
The British pound inched up to $1.6207 from $1.6197. The dollar climbed to 1.4260 Swiss francs from 1.4180 francs but was unchanged at Canadian $1.3443.
Speaking to reporters after addressing the American Association of Retired Persons, Rubin brushed aside U.S. automakers' complaints about the strength of the dollar.
The automakers have repeatedly voiced concern that the sharp dollar rally against the yen is hurting their competitiveness against Japanese car manufacturers.
Rubin said the key to competitiveness is efficiency and stressed that the administration should not use the dollar as an instrument of trade policy.

"With Rubin talking about the dollar not being used as a tool of trade policy ... there was some buying of dollars for yen after that statement was made," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank Ltd. in New York.

German newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reported that United Nations inspectors had discovered that Iraq has continued to develop missiles, in contravention of U.N. resolutions ending the 1991 Gulf War.
The newspaper said the United States was contemplating a possible punitive missile strike against Iraq as a result.
"That's what squeezed the market up from 1.6425 (marks) up to 1.6460 or so," said Steven Walker, a senior trader at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in New York.

The State Department denied any such intentions, saying there was no reason for heightened concern about military action against Iraq. U.N. officials and knowledgable diplomats also dismissed the newspaper report.
